nameStory: The American Robin got its name from early European settlers who were homesick for the familiar European Robin back home. Both birds share that cheerful reddish-orange breast, so the settlers borrowed the name for this New World bird, even though they're not actually close relatives at all!
description: The American Robin is one of New England's most familiar and beloved songbirds, roughly the size of a blue jay with a plump, rounded body. Adults sport a distinctive rusty-red to orange breast, dark gray-black head and back, and a bright yellow bill. They're members of the thrush family, and you'll often see them hopping across lawns with an upright, alert posture, pausing to cock their heads and listen for worms underground.

idTips.label: Rusty-orange breast
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - a warm, rusty-red to bright orange chest and belly that catches sunlight beautifully. The color intensity can vary, with males typically showing richer, deeper orange tones than females.

idTips.label: Head-cocking behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their characteristic hunting pose: hopping a few steps on the ground, then stopping to tilt their head sideways, listening intently for earthworms moving beneath the soil. This alert, focused posture is unmistakably robin.

idTips.label: Bright yellow bill
idTips.description: A cheerful yellow-orange beak that stands out against their dark head. In good light, this golden bill color is quite striking and helps distinguish them from other similar-sized birds.

idTips.label: Gray-black head and back
idTips.description: Dark slate-gray to blackish coloring on the head, wings, and back that contrasts sharply with the bright breast. Males tend to have deeper, more blackish tones while females appear more grayish.

idTips.label: White undertail coverts
idTips.description: Look for bright white feathers under the tail that flash conspicuously when the bird flies or fans its tail. This white patch creates a helpful contrast against the darker back and wings.

idTips.label: Dawn chorus song
idTips.description: One of the first birds you'll hear singing in the pre-dawn darkness, their song is a series of clear, liquid phrases that sound like 'cheerily-cheer-up-cheerio.' Each phrase is distinct and repeated in a pattern that's both musical and conversational.

habitat: American Robins thrive in a wide variety of New England habitats, from suburban lawns and parks to woodland edges, orchards, and golf courses. They prefer areas with short grass or bare ground for foraging, combined with nearby trees or shrubs for nesting and roosting. You'll find them from sea level to mountain elevations, often associated with human-modified landscapes that provide the perfect mix of open ground and scattered trees.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity begins in March as robins return from southern wintering grounds, singing enthusiastically at dawn and beginning their famous nest-building with mud-lined cups. Look for them pulling earthworms from newly thawed soil and engaging in territorial disputes.
seasonality.summer: Busy with multiple broods, adults constantly hunt for insects and worms to feed nestlings. Young robins appear with heavily spotted breasts, begging noisily from their parents throughout neighborhoods and parks.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks form as they prepare for migration, often seen feeding on fruit trees and berry bushes. Their behavior becomes more social and less territorial as family groups join together.
seasonality.winter: Many migrate south, but some remain in New England, shifting their diet to fruits and berries. Winter robins often appear in flocks in areas with abundant food sources and shelter.

funFact: American Robins are North America's most abundant landbird with an estimated 370 million individuals - that means there are more robins on the continent than there are people in the United States!
confusionNotes: Young robins with their heavily spotted breasts can confuse beginners, but look for that telltale rusty wash on the chest and the characteristic ground-hopping behavior. Adult robins are rarely confused with other species due to their distinctive orange breast, though female robins are paler than males. Remember: if it's hopping on the ground with an orange breast and yellow bill, it's almost certainly a robin!
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the name 'robin' with Europe's beloved Robin Redbreast, American Robins belong to completely different bird families and aren't closely related at all. The European Robin is actually more like a flycatcher, while our American Robin is a true thrush, related to bluebirds and other ground-foraging songbirds.
compareHints: While two other Turdus species (Redwing and Fieldfare) occasionally appear in New England as rare vagrants, American Robin is easily distinguished by its solid orange breast - the others have streaked or spotted underparts. Among other thrushes in our region, robins are much larger and more boldly colored than the brown, spotted Wood Thrush or Hermit Thrush, and they spend much more time foraging on open ground rather than in dense forest understory.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the American Robin, which has a solid rusty-red breast, the Redwing has rusty-red only on its wings and flanks with a spotted white breast.
Compared to its cousin the American Robin, fieldfares have that distinctive gray head contrasting with a brown (not gray) back, much heavier breast spotting, and white underwing patches.
